front_blocks.md: Define **fractional distillation**.

back_blocks.md: **Fractional distillation** is the industrial process used to separate **crude oil** into groups of hydrocarbons called **fractions**, based on differences in their **boiling points**.

cards.back_md: **Fractional distillation** is the industrial process used to separate **crude oil** into groups of hydrocarbons called **fractions**, based on differences in their **boiling points**.

front_blocks.md: In a fractionating column, hydrocarbons with **higher** boiling points condense **..........** the column, while those with **lower** boiling points condense **..........** .

back_blocks.md: In a fractionating column, hydrocarbons with **higher** boiling points condense **towards the bottom of** the column, while those with **lower** boiling points condense **towards the top**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Crude oil is a pure substance made up of a single hydrocarbon.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Crude oil is a **mixture of hydrocarbons**. The different hydrocarbons are separated into fractions by **fractional distillation** because they have different boiling points.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

Crude oil is a pure substance made up of a single hydrocarbon.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

Crude oil is a **mixture of hydrocarbons**. The different hydrocarbons are separated into fractions by **fractional distillation** because they have different boiling points.

front_blocks.md: What property of a hydrocarbon fraction determines where it condenses in the fractionating column?

back_blocks.md: A fraction condenses at the point in the column where the temperature matches its **boiling point**. Fractions with **higher boiling points** (longer chains) condense lower down; those with **lower boiling points** (shorter chains) rise higher before condensing.

front_blocks.md: Define **fraction** (crude oil).

back_blocks.md: A **fraction** is a group of hydrocarbons separated from crude oil during **fractional distillation**, each consisting of molecules with similar **chain lengths** and **boiling points**.

front_blocks.md: Name the six main fractions obtained from crude oil, in order from shortest to longest carbon chain.

back_blocks.md: The six main fractions are:

1. (Shortest) Refinery gas
2. Gasoline
3. Kerosene
4. Diesel
5. Fuel oil
6. (Longest) Bitumen

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Kerosene is used as a fuel for jet aircraft.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
**Kerosene** (also called **paraffin**) is the crude oil fraction used as **jet fuel**. It has a carbon chain length of roughly 12–16 atoms.

front_blocks.md: What is **bitumen** used for and why is it suitable for that use?

back_blocks.md: **Bitumen** is used for **surfacing roads and roofs**. Its very long carbon chains (70+ C atoms) make it extremely **viscous** and solid at room temperature, giving it good waterproofing and load-bearing properties.

front_blocks.md: Why does volatility decrease as the carbon chain length of a hydrocarbon fraction increases?

back_blocks.md: Longer chains have stronger **intermolecular forces** between molecules. More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so the fraction is less likely to vaporise, making it less **volatile**.

front_blocks.md: Define **fuel**.

back_blocks.md: A **fuel** is a substance that, when burned, releases **heat energy** in an **exothermic** reaction.

back_blocks.md: **Complete combustion** of a hydrocarbon occurs when there is **excess** oxygen, producing **carbon dioxide** and water.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons can produce carbon particulates (soot).

back_blocks.md: **True.**
**Incomplete combustion** occurs when oxygen supply is insufficient. Products can include **carbon monoxide**, **unburned hydrocarbons** and **carbon particulates** (**soot**), as well as water.

front_blocks.md: What gases are released when fossil fuels burn and contribute to atmospheric pollution?

back_blocks.md: Burning fossil fuels releases **carbon dioxide**, **carbon monoxide**, **oxides of nitrogen** and **oxides of sulfur**. Incomplete combustion also produces **unburned hydrocarbons** and **carbon particulates**.

front_blocks.md: Define **carbon monoxide**.

back_blocks.md: **Carbon monoxide** (CO) is a colourless, odourless, toxic gas produced during the **incomplete combustion** of carbon-containing fuels.

front_blocks.md: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous to humans?

back_blocks.md: **Carbon monoxide** reduces the **capacity of blood to transport oxygen** around the body. Because it is colourless, odourless and tasteless, it can be inhaled without detection.

front_blocks.md: Where is incomplete combustion most likely to occur in everyday situations?

back_blocks.md: **Incomplete combustion** occurs where oxygen supply is limited, such as in **boilers**, **stoves** and **internal combustion engines** in vehicles.

front_blocks.md: Define **nitrogen oxides**.

back_blocks.md: **Nitrogen oxides** are a group of compounds (including NO and NO<sub>2</sub>) formed when **nitrogen** and **oxygen** from air react together at the high temperatures reached inside **car engines**.

back_blocks.md: Car engines reach high enough **temperatures** and **pressures** for nitrogen and oxygen in air to react with each other, forming nitrogen oxides such as NO and NO<sub>2</sub>.

front_blocks.md: Define **acid rain**.

back_blocks.md: **Acid rain** is precipitation with a pH lower than normal, caused by **sulfur dioxide** and **nitrogen oxides** dissolving in rainwater to form **sulfuric acid** and **nitric acid**.

front_blocks.md: Define **cracking**.

back_blocks.md: **Cracking** is an industrial process in which long-chain hydrocarbon molecules are broken down into shorter-chain **alkanes** and **alkenes** using heat and a catalyst.

cards.front_md: Define **cracking**.
cards.back_md: **Cracking** is an industrial process in which long-chain hydrocarbon molecules are broken down into shorter-chain **alkanes** and **alkenes** using heat and a catalyst.

front_blocks.md: Why is cracking necessary in the oil industry?

back_blocks.md: **Demand** for short-chain fractions such as petrol exceeds their **supply** from fractional distillation, so cracking converts surplus long-chain fractions into more useful shorter-chain products.

cards.front_md: Why is cracking necessary in the oil industry?
cards.back_md: **Demand** for short-chain fractions such as petrol exceeds their **supply** from fractional distillation, so cracking converts surplus long-chain fractions into more useful shorter-chain products.

front_blocks.md: In catalytic cracking, hydrocarbon vapours pass over a hot catalyst of **..........** at a temperature of **..........** °C.

back_blocks.md: In catalytic cracking, hydrocarbon vapours pass over a hot catalyst of **aluminium oxide** at a temperature of **600–700** °C.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Cracking is an endothermic reaction.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
**Cracking** requires a continuous input of heat energy to break the covalent bonds in long-chain hydrocarbons, making it an **endothermic** reaction.

cards.front_md:

Cracking is an endothermic reaction.

front_blocks.md: What types of product are formed when a long-chain alkane is cracked?

back_blocks.md: Cracking produces a mixture of shorter-chain **alkanes** and **alkenes**. The alkenes contain carbon-carbon double bonds and the alkanes contain only single bonds.

front_blocks.md: Define **alkene**.

back_blocks.md: An **alkene** is an **unsaturated** hydrocarbon containing at least one carbon-carbon **double bond**, produced alongside shorter **alkanes** during the **cracking** of long-chain hydrocarbons.

front_blocks.md: What temperature range is used in catalytic cracking?

back_blocks.md: Catalytic cracking is carried out at **600–700 °C**, which is hot enough to vaporise the hydrocarbon molecules before they contact the catalyst.
